t: #3566 Partition Array into Two Equal Product Subsets
o: We must split distinct positive integers into two non-empty groups whose products both equal `target`. Since every element lands in exactly one group, if one subset has product `target`, the other automatically must too — so we really just search for one proper, non-empty subset with product `target`. Example 1: {3,8} gives 24 and the complement {1,6,4} also gives 24. Example 2: no subset of [2,5,3,7] multiplies to 15 together with its complement doing the same. With n ≤ 12 there are only 2^12 = 4096 subsets, so exhaustive enumeration is intended; products can reach 100^12 ≈ 10^24, so 64-bit languages must guard against overflow while multiplying.
k: Searching for one subset with product target suffices — the complement then also has product target because the total product is target².
n ≤ 12 makes bitmask enumeration (4096 subsets) or pruned DFS both viable.
In fixed-width languages, check `product > target / x` before multiplying to avoid overflow.

a.i: Try every non-trivial bitmask over the array. For each mask compute the product of chosen elements and of the complement; accept if both equal target. Early-abort multiplying once a partial product would exceed target keeps values within 64 bits.
s: Iterate masks from 1 to 2^n − 2 (non-empty, proper subsets).
For each mask accumulate both products, aborting a side if it would exceed target.
Return true when both products equal target.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — about 4096 · 12 operations at most.

a.i: Recursively decide each element: put it in subset A (multiply p) or subset B (multiply q). Since all values are positive, once p or q exceeds target that branch can never recover, so we prune aggressively. Sorting descending makes branches fail fast.
s: DFS(i, p, q): prune if p > target or q > target.
At i = n, succeed iff p == q == target; otherwise branch on placing nums[i] in either subset.
a.t: O(2^n) worst case, but pruning on exceeded products cuts most branches in practice.

w: Use bitmask enumeration for simplicity — n ≤ 12 guarantees it passes. Pitfalls: forgetting the subset must be proper and non-empty (exclude mask 0 and full mask), and 64-bit overflow in C++/Java/JavaScript (guard with division before multiplying). Follow-ups: what if elements repeat, or you must return the actual subsets?
